extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in censorship, media regulation, and Islamic societies
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive survey of censorship practices, laws, and incidents across Islamic-majority and other countries where Islam influences censorship decisions; documents legal standards, state and non‑state enforcement, and examples. Useful for comparative study and background on how religious, political, and social rationales shape restrictions on speech and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIC call for ban on denigration of Muhammad
rubrics_metrics.description: The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has lobbied at the international level for a global ban on speech criticizing Muhammad; called for a categorical ban on stuff that could be deemed as denigration of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an intergovernmental lobbying effort aiming to criminalize speech critical of religion at the international level; contrasted with Western free-speech positions which opposed the resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blasphemy / prohibition on insulting prophets
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal or constitutional provisions prohibiting 'insult or abuse of all religious messengers and prophets' are used as justification for censorship (example: Egyptian Constitution's Article quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as the constitutional/legal basis used by some states or lawmakers to justify censorship of materials deemed insulting to religion or prophets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of public order, decency, or morality
rubrics_metrics.description: States may restrict freedom of speech when content is seen to threaten 'public order, decency or morality' (example: India's constitution allows 'reasonable restrictions' for these interests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a broad, catch-all legal standard to justify bans or censorship of books, films, or other media that cause emotional distress or communal tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious police / enforcement of Sharia
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious police or similar institutions enforce Islamic Sharia law and censor behavior and media deemed un-Islamic (examples: Saudi religious police, Ministries of Virtue and Vice in Afghanistan/Taliban).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational enforcement mechanism that can impose bans, arrests, or restrictions on cultural practices, media, dress, and public behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication review by state cultural ministries
rubrics_metrics.description: Government ministries (e.g., Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance) review written works and films before allowing publication or distribution; the process can involve multiple officials and long delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the bureaucratic censorship process (e.g., Iran: three separate officials inspect works; review can take months to years) and the ability to alter/delete lines or scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of specific depictions (women, physical contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censors forbid depiction of women singing or dancing, require actresses to conceal hair, and suppress direct physical contact between opposite sexes (example: Iranian film censorship rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific content restrictions derived from moral/religious norms that shape permitted portrayals in film and television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banning of entire media categories (films, music, female voices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blanket bans on categories of media have been imposed (example: Taliban's blanket ban on all films and videos; bans on music and women speaking on TV/radio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents the most severe form of censorship where whole media forms are prohibited rather than selectively edited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking or filtering internet platforms and websites
rubrics_metrics.description: States monitor and filter websites accused of hosting anti-Islamic content, and may block platforms (examples: Pakistan/other states blocking YouTube, Facebook; blocking Google/Gmail in Iran).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical censorship via ISPs/telecom regulators (e.g., Pakistan Telecommunication Authority) used to restrict online access to contentious content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of criminal law and legal bans against specific works
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments outright ban books, films or other works for perceived attacks on Islam or for promoting communal disharmony (examples: bans on The Satanic Verses in India and other works in various countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal prohibition of distribution or possession of named works, sometimes resulting in seizures, visa cancellations, or legal action against authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatwas and extrajudicial religious judgments as censorship/enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious rulings (fatwas) have been issued calling for punishment, ostracism, or violence against creators of perceived offensive works (example: fatwas against The Satanic Verses author and against participants in Innocence of Muslims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-state religious edicts that create pressure, threats, or direct calls for harm, leading to self-censorship or capitulation by publishers and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship driven by threats of violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Creators, publishers, broadcasters, and platforms practice self-censorship in non-Islamic countries due to threats of violence or the risk of violent protest (examples: Random House canceling publication; Comedy Central censoring South Park episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the chilling effect: fear of retribution (death threats, riots) leads actors to avoid publishing or to alter content even where legal protections exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship justified on national security or international peace grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that provocative insults are 'a threat to international peace and security and the sanctity of life' have been used to argue for restrictions on speech (as quoted by an OIC official).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames certain speech as a security risk to justify domestic or international regulation/censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship for moral/religious propriety (disturbing public morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content judged to 'disturb public order and threaten proper morals' (example: Tunisia fining broadcaster for airing Persepolis) is censored or penalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by regulators to target material they see as violating prevailing moral/religious standards, often resulting in fines or broadcasting restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of market/publisher safety concerns to cancel publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may cancel or delay publication citing 'very real possibility of major danger' or 'national security' concerns if a work could provoke violent backlash (example: Random House canceling The Jewel of Medina).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial/self-protective censorship where institutions withdraw support to protect staff, property, or public safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal statutes banning content deemed 'defaming' or 'anti-national'
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws that ban content accused of 'defaming the Arab nation' or promoting 'reactionary, chauvinistic, populistic, racialist or rationalistic ideas' have been used to justify film and media bans (example: Iraqi Law on the Censorship of Foreign Films of 1973).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadly worded legal provisions that empower authorities to ban diverse content on political, cultural, or ideological grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censoring imagery considered offensive (e.g., pig images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper editions have censored images (example: pig faces blacked out in Malaysian edition of International New York Times) when images are considered offensive to religious sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial/press-level self-censorship or state pressure to remove or alter images deemed disrespectful.

rubrics_metrics.name: State promotion of Islamic programming and religious administration
rubrics_metrics.description: States may subsidize religious programming, promote official muftiates, and use state-controlled religious bodies to smooth connections between state and believers, accompanying content restrictions (example: Uzbekistan's promotion of state muftiyat and religious programming while banning certain adverts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how positive promotion of state-sanctioned religious content can accompany prohibitions on other material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship used as outreach or co-option of Islamist actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments may implement Islamic censorship as part of outreach to Islamist groups or to co-opt their demands (example: Hosni Mubarak revising codes and implementing censorship to take heat off Islamist activists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political strategy: adopting or accommodating censorship demands to manage domestic political pressures.
